tip: Vouloir takes a bare infinitive – no 'to' in between: 'veut partir' is want + leave, straight through. Pouvoir works the same: il peut partir.
Ouvrir ends in -ir but conjugates like an -er verb: it's 'j'ouvre', not j'ouvris. Couvrir and offrir do the same.
Regarder already means 'look at' – the 'at' is baked in: 'regardez la télévision', never regarder à. Écouter (listen to) works the same way.
For things, adorer is 'love' while aimer only reaches 'like': 'adorent le chocolat' is stronger than aiment. (For people, aimer already means love.)
Passer is 'to spend' for time, not money: 'passe ses vacances' = spends his holidays. Spending money is dépenser.
French keeps the article for likes in general: 'aimez le café' is literally 'like the coffee', where English just drops the 'the'.
Des is the plural 'some' English usually skips: 'prend des photos' = takes (some) photos. French won't drop it – bare prend photos is wrong.
A number stands in for the article: 'deux enfants', never deux des enfants. The count already does the article's job.
Vous is both plural 'you' and the polite singular. 'Vous pouvez répéter ?' is the safe form with a stranger; tu would sound too familiar.
'Je veux un café' is blunt – fine among friends, pushy to a waiter. To order, soften it to 'je voudrais' (I'd like).
Connaître is knowing-by-familiarity – people, places, songs: 'connais cette chanson'. Knowing a fact or how-to would be savoir.
Obéir needs à where English obeys directly: 'obéit à ses parents' is literally 'obeys to his parents'.
Entrer needs dans – you don't enter a place, you enter INTO it: 'entrez dans le magasin', never entrer le magasin.
In speech a rising tone alone makes a question: 'Tu peux venir demain ?' keeps ordinary statement word order – no inversion required.
Unsure whether to use tu or vous? Start with vous, as in 'Vous avez'. A wrong tu can offend; a wrong vous just sounds polite.
Au is à + le fused into one word: 'allez au marché' = go to the market. The two always merge.
'On va au supermarché': on is spoken French for 'we', but the verb stays in the he/she form – on va, never on allons.
Chercher already means 'look for' – the 'for' is inside it: 'cherche la gare', never chercher pour. Attendre (wait for) is the same.
Réfléchir needs à for whatever you think about: 'réfléchis à la question' = think about the question.
On has a second life as impersonal 'one/they': 'On fait les courses' can mean we do the shopping, or people in general do. Context decides.
Venir de + infinitive means 'just did', not 'come to': 'venons de finir' = we just finished. The de is what flips it to the recent past.
'Viens de Lyon' means come FROM Lyon – an origin. But venir de + a verb means 'just did': je viens de manger = I just ate. The next word decides.
English 'leave' splits in French: sortir is going out for the evening ('sors ce soir'); quitter is leaving a place or person behind.
Body features take the definite article, not 'some': 'a les yeux bleus' is literally 'has THE blue eyes', never des yeux bleus.
Age is something you HAVE in French: 'j'ai vingt-cinq ans' is literally 'I have twenty-five years'. Être here would be wrong.
'À le' is never said in French – it must contract to au: 'vais au cinéma', not à le cinéma.
Belle comes before its noun: 'une belle maison', not maison belle. A few short common adjectives (beau, grand, petit) lead like this.
'Je suis' is both 'I am' (être) and 'I follow' (suivre). Here it's following: 'je suis la leçon' = I follow the lesson, not I am it.
Il me suffit works impersonally: 'il me suffit d'une heure' is literally 'it suffices me an hour' = an hour is enough for me. The amount you need takes de.
Sensations are things you HAVE in French: 'ont soif' = have thirst, not 'are thirsty'. Cold and fear too: avoir froid, avoir peur.
'Nous avons faim' is literally 'we have hunger'. Watch out – 'je suis faim' would mean you ARE hunger itself.
Flipping verb and subject makes a formal question: 'Avez-vous un menu' = do you have a menu. Casual speech just says vous avez un menu ?
Du is de + le fused: 'sort du bureau' = leaves the office, literally 'out OF the office'. De le is never said.
In speech, on almost always replaces nous: 'on mange' for 'we eat'. Nous now sounds formal or written.
Weather 'makes' in French: 'il fait beau' is literally 'it makes nice' = it's nice out. Cold and hot too: il fait froid, il fait chaud.
Negation wraps the verb in two parts: 'ne manges pas'. In casual speech the ne drops – you'll hear tu manges pas – but writing keeps it.
Before a vowel, vieux becomes vieil: 'un vieil homme', never vieux homme. It's purely to avoid two vowel sounds clashing.
'Te lèves' is literally 'you raise yourself' – a reflexive verb turns the action back on you. The pronoun must match: je me lève, tu te lèves.
Ton matches the noun's gender, not the owner's: 'ton frère' is right whether a man or woman speaks – frère is masculine, so ton.
De shrinks to d' before a vowel: 'besoin d'un stylo'. Two words can't sit vowel-to-vowel, so de un becomes d'un.
Adjectives split around the noun: size first, colour after – 'un gros chien noir' is a big dog black. Gros leads, noir trails.
Weather takes the partitive 'some': 'du vent' is literally 'some wind' = it's windy. Sun and fog too: du soleil, du brouillard.
'Il y a' covers both 'there is' and 'there are' – it never changes for number: 'il y a trop de bruit', il y a trois livres.
Beau becomes bel before a vowel: 'un beau pays' but un bel été. Vieux does the same: vieil homme.
A few adjectives sit before the noun, and you can stack them: 'un joli petit village' puts both joli and petit up front, unlike most French adjectives.
